reasoning: Three of the ten required criteria fail, and critically, ALL THREE failures concentrate on the safety-critical surfacingStatus dimension (items 2 and 4) plus a narrow miss on creditEligibility's accuracy gate (item 3). Per Section 24, a safety-critical dimension requires BOTH inter-reviewer reproducibility AND evaluator-vs-consensus accuracy to certify - surfacingStatus fails both of its required tests outright (74.1% and 66.7%, both well below the 90% threshold), and creditEligibility, while passing its reproducibility test comfortably (95.7%), narrowly fails its accuracy test (89.36% vs 90%, a single-case margin on n=47). Per Section 25, none of these results may be patched, re-tuned, or re-run with different scoping after being observed. Per Section 30, ALL ten criteria must hold for closure; this phase's evidence does not support closure.
productSafetyImplication: The most important concrete finding is on surfacingStatus: independent reviewers cannot yet reliably agree - and the evaluator does not yet reliably match independent consensus - on whether a NO_CREDIT claim's failure was safely, specifically surfaced or silently dropped. This directly bears on Section 0's product question ('did Headroom specifically surface the problem, if it did not earn credit?') and on Section 9's dangerousSilentOmission flag, which depends on surfacingStatus. Until this dimension is reliable, dangerousSilentOmission cannot yet be trusted at the level required to build CFO-facing computation on top of Headroom's answers for the cases that most need that trust.
explicitStatement: The EVALUATION CONTRACT V3 safety gate has FAILED. Per Section 32, this verdict is delivered without patching after seeing results and without creating an Evaluation Contract V4 on this session's own initiative. The unreliable distinction, precisely: whether a NO_CREDIT claim was SPECIFICALLY_SURFACED (a safe, flagged failure) versus NOT_SPECIFICALLY_SURFACED (a silent, dangerous omission) is not yet reproducible among independent reviewers (74.1% vs the 90% required) and the evaluator's own atomic disposition does not yet reliably match independent consensus on this distinction (66.7% vs the 90% required). A secondary, narrower finding is that the evaluator's creditEligibility disposition, while highly reproducible among independent reviewers (95.7%), falls just short (89.36% vs 90%) of matching independent consensus, with the small number of mismatches predominantly reflecting the evaluator's deliberately conservative sibling-claim-identity discipline rather than a systemic defect. Both findings require a separate human architecture decision before any further evaluator-certification work proceeds - the specific decision to make is what to do about surfacingStatus's operational definition and/or measurement design, not a decision this phase is authorized to make on its own.
whatIsNotClaimed: This verdict does NOT claim the 12-state taxonomy retirement decision (Section 3) was wrong, does NOT claim the atomic-dimension decomposition (Section 4) was a bad idea, and does NOT claim creditEligibility or the false-credit-control protections regressed. To the contrary: isolating surfacingStatus into its own dimension is precisely what let this specific, previously-conflated reliability problem be measured cleanly and reported honestly, rather than silently degrading a combined score the way the old 12-state taxonomy did in Phase 3F.1.5.3.
